action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; the coagulation profile also bears on the subdural bleed [ACG_HE_2026]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute all AMS to HE and forego neuroimaging — focal right-sided signs (pronator drift, hyperreflexia) and unilateral headache are not explained by HE alone and mandate CT head to exclude structural pathology.

Do not be falsely reassured by partial lactulose improvement — incomplete recovery with persistent focal deficits in a coagulopathic cirrhotic with a recent fall is a strong indicator of concurrent structural pathology.
Do not perform LP before CT head has excluded and neurosurgery has cleared the intracranial mass effect from the SDH — LP in the setting of mass effect and midline shift risks herniation.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for agitation or sedating opioids for headache — both precipitate and prolong HE in cirrhosis.
Do not initiate anticoagulation or antiplatelet agents without neurosurgical clearance — the SDH with coagulopathy is at risk for expansion.
Do not anchor on ammonia 74 as confirmation of pure HE — ammonia elevation supports HE but does not exclude a concurrent structural lesion.
required_recommendations: Obtain non-contrast CT head urgently — focal right-sided signs (pronator drift, asymmetric hyperreflexia) and unilateral headache in a coagulopathic cirrhotic mandate imaging to exclude structural intracranial pathology; do not defer imaging based on partial lactulose response.

Neurosurgery evaluation of the chronic left-convexity SDH — the right pronator drift and right arm hyperreflexia are contralateral to the left SDH, consistent with mass effect; establish serial CT monitoring schedule and surgical threshold.
Treat the UTI precipitant — urine culture-directed antibiotic therapy; nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (no allergy documented) first-line per susceptibilities.
Correct coagulopathy: target INR <1.5 and platelets >100 x10^9/L before any invasive neurosurgical intervention; avoid anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents while SDH is present.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more and correct the magnesium, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis; hold furosemide and spironolactone while overt HE and the electrolyte disorder persist (EASL 2018).
Avoid benzodiazepines and sedating opioids, which worsen HE; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for the headache.
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.
Hold metformin during the acute illness (decompensated cirrhosis with infection) and monitor capillary glucose, using insulin if needed.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 18, 14 months abstinent (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE or SDH workup in this case.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE or acute SDH workup; reversible/structural causes have been identified.
FDG PET has no role in this workup; metabolic encephalopathy and structural SDH have been identified and do not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 18), precipitated by urinary tract infection, with concurrent chronic left-convexity subdural hematoma (9 mm, 3 mm rightward midline shift) from cirrhotic coagulopathy and a minor fall, identified by neuroimaging prompted by focal right-sided signs and an incomplete response to lactulose.

differential.diagnosis: Chronic subdural hematoma as a concurrent contributor to the altered mental status (not the primary cause)
differential.key_features: CT shows a 9 mm left-convexity chronic SDH with 3 mm midline shift, explaining the right pronator drift, right-arm hyperreflexia and left-sided headache; coagulopathy and the recent fall give the mechanism. The global encephalopathy with asterixis, the UTI and the partial response to lactulose point to HE as the main cause.

differential.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy alone (pure HE without structural lesion)
differential.key_features: UTI precipitant and asterixis support HE, but the CT shows a concurrent chronic SDH that explains the focal signs, so HE alone is excluded.

differential.diagnosis: Septic encephalopathy from urinary source (as primary diagnosis rather than HE precipitant)
differential.key_features: Pyuria, nitrites and an E. coli urine culture confirm the UTI, but she is not septic (temperature 37.8 °C, HR 96, BP 138/84, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, blood cultures sterile) and has asterixis; in cirrhosis the infection precipitates HE rather than causing a separate septic encephalopathy.
Ascites present, but the ascitic PMN count is 64 cells/mm3, below the 250 cells/mm3 threshold, and the culture is sterile; the urinary tract is the infective source.

differential.diagnosis: Ischemic stroke (left MCA territory given right-sided signs)
differential.key_features: Right arm pronator drift and hyperreflexia raise the possibility of a left hemispheric stroke; the CT shows the SDH and no infarct, and the SDH explains the right-sided signs.

Fluctuating consciousness in a cirrhotic with a cortical subdural collection; no witnessed seizure, twitching or gaze deviation, and consciousness improved with lactulose. An EEG, if obtained, shows diffuse slowing without epileptiform discharges.

key_clinical_evidence: Focal neurological signs (right pronator drift, asymmetric right-arm hyperreflexia) with a unilateral headache are not features of typical HE and warrant urgent neuroimaging regardless of the ammonia or the lactulose response (ACG 2026 recommendation 6: imaging for a new focal deficit, head trauma or no response to treatment).

The laterality is internally consistent: the chronic SDH is on the LEFT convexity, on the side of the headache, producing a right-sided motor deficit through contralateral mass effect, unlike the symmetric signs of HE.

A partial response to lactulose does not exclude a second cause: HE can co-exist with, and partially improve alongside, a concurrent structural lesion; an incomplete recovery should increase, not decrease, the suspicion of an additional cause.

Cirrhotic coagulopathy (INR 1.8, platelets 98, low fibrinogen) combined with an unwitnessed minor fall provides the mechanism for the chronic SDH and is a recognized risk for intracranial hemorrhage that warrants imaging.

The UTI is the HE precipitant (dysuria, pyuria, positive nitrites, leukocytosis, temperature 37.8 °C, E. coli on urine culture), not the SDH: both require simultaneous treatment, antibiotics for the precipitant and neurosurgical management for the structural lesion.
A lumbar puncture is not indicated: there is no meningism, the CT explains the focal signs, and with a 9 mm SDH and midline shift an LP would risk herniation.
Child-Pugh C (10: bilirubin 2.4 2, albumin 2.9 2, INR 1.8 2, mild ascites 2, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 18 (creatinine 1.0, bilirubin 2.4, INR 1.8, sodium 134)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Partial improvement is consistent with HE responding to lactulose, but the persistent focal right-sided signs and incomplete recovery to GCS 15 mandate neuroimaging — both diagnoses (HE and SDH) can co-exist and must be addressed independently.
red_herrings.data_point: Partial improvement in GCS from 13 to 14 after 24 hours of lactulose escalation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret partial lactulose response as evidence of resolving HE and discontinue further structural workup, missing the concurrent chronic SDH.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ammonia elevation supports HE (per AASLD, it is supportive but not diagnostic and correlates poorly with grade); it does not exclude a concurrent structural lesion. Focal signs mandate CT regardless of ammonia level.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all AMS to the elevated ammonia and treat as straightforward HE without imaging, anchoring on biochemical confirmation of HE.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: overt HE grade II with UTI precipitant in a cirrhotic woman — partial lactulose improvement falsely reassures, but a subtle right pronator drift, asymmetric right-arm hyperreflexia, and unilateral headache prompt mandatory CT head revealing a chronic left-convexity SDH (9 mm, 3 mm midline shift) from cirrhotic coagulopathy plus a minor unwitnessed fall. Tests resistance to HE anchoring when structural lesion is concurrent.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Four required investigations (core labs with coagulation, CT head, blood and urine cultures with diagnostic paracentesis) and a required medication review; two grounded red herrings (partial lactulose response, raised ammonia); concurrent HE and chronic SDH requires the synthesis of a focal exam sign, coagulopathy, a fall and an incomplete recovery; resisting anchoring on HE is the core challenge.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 62-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14 at her last hepatology review) and a prior hepatic encephalopathy episode 9 months ago, now on lactulose and rifaximin secondary prophylaxis, brought to the emergency department by her daughter for a 3-day history of worsening confusion, irritability, and difficulty performing routine tasks. Her daughter reports she found her mother disoriented and unable to manage her medications two days ago. The patient complains of a mild left-temporal headache present for 2 days. She denies hematemesis or melena. Her daughter reports she noticed some dysuria 5 days ago but the patient had not sought care. On review of records, she was seen at an urgent care 10 days ago for a fall at home that was unwitnessed — she was assessed and discharged without imaging. She has been adherent to lactulose and rifaximin based on pill counts. In the emergency department her lactulose was increased and given by nasogastric tube. Over the following 24 hours her mental status improved only partially (GCS 13 to 14): she remained mildly confused, continued to report headache, and a right pronator drift with asymmetric right-arm hyperreflexia was noted on repeat neurological examination. The examination below is that repeat examination.
